speaker: Doctor
text:
Good morning, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are presenting with blisters on your forearm and ulcers on mucosal surfaces; can you tell me exactly where these ulcers are located and if they are painful?

REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count, Comprehensive Metabolic Panel, HIV, Syphilis Serology, RPR.
REQUEST IMAGES: Dermatology photos of forearm lesions and mucosal involvement.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CBC: Within normal limits; Comprehensive Metabolic Panel: Not provided in current data; HIV: Not provided in current data; Syphilis Serology: Not provided in current data; RPR: Not provided in current data. Note: Based on clinical findings (mucosal ulcers, flaccid blisters, Nikolsky sign positive, acantholysis, and desmoglein antibodies), the clinical picture is highly suggestive of Pemphigus Vulgaris.

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old female. The patient reports the appearance of blisters on her forearm 3 days ago, accompanied by pain in her left cheek when eating and pain during sexual intercourse for the past week. She has been hiking in the woods recently but denies contact with poison ivy. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis, recently started taking captopril, and discontinued meloxicam 2 weeks ago. Family history includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease.

speaker: Patient
text: includes pernicious anemia and Graves' disease.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Hypertension, osteoarthritis. Social history: Has started hiking in the woods on weekends. No relevant travel history.

speaker: Patient
text: No recent illnesses, denies fever, respiratory symptoms, or gastrointestinal symptoms. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Cellulitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The previous suggestion of cellulitis does not fit your presentation of blisters and mucosal ulcers, as cellulitis is a skin infection that does not typically cause mucosal lesions or blistering. Let's clarify the details: are these ulcers located in your mouth, eyes, or genitals, and do you have any history of similar outbreaks or a diagnosis of Behçet's disease or pemphigus vulgaris?

REQUEST TEST: Anti-desmoglein antibodies, ANA, ESR, CRP.
REQUEST IMAGES: Close-up views of the forearm blisters and any visible mucosal ulcers.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Anti-desmoglein antibodies: Presence of desmoglein antibodies; ANA: Not provided in current data; ESR: Not provided in current data; CRP: Not provided in current data.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The presence of desmoglein antibodies is highly specific for an autoimmune blistering disease; based on your forearm blisters and mucosal ulcers, do these lesions have a "dewdrop on a rose petal" appearance on the skin, and are your mouth or genital ulcers recurrent and painful?

REQUEST TEST: Indirect Immunofluorescence (Direct and Indirect).
REQUEST IMAGES: High-resolution photos showing the base of the skin blisters to check for a "dewdrop" morphology.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Direct Immunofluorescence: Intercellular IgG and C3 deposition within the epidermis; Indirect Immunofluorescence: Not provided in current data.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The positive Direct Immunofluorescence showing intercellular IgG and C3 deposition is the classic "chicken wire" pattern diagnostic for pemphigus vulgaris. Before I finalize the diagnosis, can you confirm that the skin blisters on your forearm are fragile and rupture easily, leaving shallow erosions behind?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Pemphigus Vulgaris
